Lotus — navigation options

Five ways to help people find things, compared against the people who use Lotus.

Comparison v2
9 October 2026
Mindful Design
Draft for review

For Matt, Rosie and Alexander before it is shared more widely. This draft sets out options and their trade-offs as a starting point rather than a recommendation, and the dev team's view on what is workable will shape the final choice.

The choice touches information architecture, data structure, UI, UX and brand at once, which is why it needs more than one view. Once the dev team has said what each option takes to build, the decision comes down mainly to user experience and brand fit, with build effort weighed in wherever the options differ.

The problem

The live header shows Events, Courses and a More menu holding Memberships, Teachers, Centres and the Admin panel. Items hidden under More are easy to miss, so they need visibility within the limited space in the header.

Two further pressures sit behind that. Lotus is growing beyond FPMT and the Tibetan tradition, so there will be more to find over time. And many visitors, especially newcomers, don't yet know what to search for: a search bar with no guidance or suggestions assumes people already know what's on offer.

The main question is how much guidance Lotus should offer, and where.

What everyone already agrees on

The header becomes five items: Events, Study, Retreats, Centres, Teachers. To save horizontal space, the location field stays collapsed until search is in use, and the "English" dropdown becomes a globe and a language code. That frees enough room for all five on one line. This is the structure from the IA proposal v2: three intents (Events, Study, Retreats) and two directories (Centres, Teachers).

Item todayWhere it goes
CoursesCould be renamed Study, to cover live courses, self-study, study programmes and the teaching archive (TBC after centre feedback), which can be browsed by teacher, year, language and format. "Study" is less specific than "Courses", but it carries less sense of being sold something, and it fits the free content on offer, such as any free introductory courses, videos on demand and archival material.
Centres, TeachersHeader, as plain links. Each leads to a results page with that filter applied, with page-specific sub-filters such as tradition, lineage, courses, language and continent (TBC)
MembershipsCentre pages, as a way to support them and access membership perks, and the account menu for existing members. People usually reach membership after getting to know a centre, not while browsing
Admin panelAccount menu. Anyone with an account has this menu; the Admin panel link inside it only appears for people with an admin role
English ▾Globe and language code, repeated in the account menu

Everything below is about one remaining question: what, if anything, helps people find things beyond these five links.

Five options

Most of these can be combined. Each is shown on its own first.

1 · Simple menu

Five plain links, each going to its own page. Search, filters and the homepage category icons do the rest. The header stays minimal, in line with a calm design ethos, and with the brand architecture's aim of a platform quiet enough to let each centre lead.

Pros
  • Minimal header, nothing extra to maintain
  • Matches IA v2 exactly
  • Simplest on mobile
Cons
  • Little guidance outside the homepage icons
  • Doesn't show the breadth of traditions
  • Visitors set filters themselves

2 · Mega menu

Events, Study and Retreats open a panel of shortcuts on click. Each link lands on the results page with filters already set, so a visitor reaches "weekend retreats" or "online events" in one click from any page. The dev team has confirmed the results page already accepts filters through the URL, the same way the homepage icons work. This answers decision 05 in IA v2, which asked whether hub links could land on a pre-filtered calendar.

Reference Wisdom Academy mega menu ↓ · Lotus prototype screens ↓

A prototype of this option, built from the staging design system, can be viewed in a one-minute video. Still screens are in the appendix.

The closest comparison to Lotus, Wisdom Academy from Wisdom Publications, uses a mega menu for its courses, organised by tradition (Tibetan, Theravada and Insight) and topic, with lineage filters such as Gelug and Kagyu inside (Ref. 1).

Pros
  • Shows breadth on every page
  • One-click shortcuts from anywhere
  • Room to grow as content is added
Cons
  • Dense when open
  • More labels to maintain
  • Needs a designed mobile version

3 · Suggestions when searching

When someone clicks into search, a dropdown offers a few shortcuts before they type anything: Near me, This weekend, Online, Suitable for beginners, and popular categories. Airbnb's "Where" field works this way (Ref. 2). It pairs naturally with collapsing the location field: the header is quiet at rest and only offers guidance once someone engages. It extends the search proposal, where typing already surfaces teachers, centres and programmes before any results page.

Time shortcuts such as Today and This weekend matter in every option, so they have their own section below.

Reference Airbnb search suggestions ↓

Pros
  • Header stays quiet at rest
  • Guidance appears at the moment of searching
  • Builds on the search proposal; a natural home for time shortcuts
Cons
  • Only seen by people who click into search
  • Nothing for visitors who browse without searching

The search proposal already designs what happens once someone starts typing. Option 3 covers the moment before that, when the field is empty. The difference matters for different people, as the persona walkthrough below shows.

4 · Header items as search scopes

Instead of linking to separate sections, Events, Study and Retreats become tabs that narrow one search, with "All" selected by default. Airbnb (All, Homes, Experiences, Services) and Booking.com both do this (Ref. 3). The scopes are the same as the search proposal's scope chips (All, Events, Study, Retreats, Centres, Teachers), which sit on the results page. Moving them into the header would change the IA v2 model, where Study and Retreats are hubs that hold undated content too, not just filters on one search.

Reference Airbnb search scopes ↓

Pros
  • One search model throughout
  • Familiar from Airbnb and Booking.com
  • Matches the search proposal's scope chips
Cons
  • Changes the IA v2 hub model
  • Can pull search into a larger, central role
  • Undated hub content is harder to reach

5 · Shortcut links at the bottom of the page

Rows of link chips at the end of the homepage, and possibly of event pages: by time, by place, by category. Eventbrite uses "Things to do around [city]" chips (Ref. 4); Airbnb has a tabbed "Inspiration" grid (Ref. 5). Eventbrite's time chips are covered under time shortcuts below. The shortcuts stay out of the header and appear where someone who scrolled without finding anything is ready for them. Each link is also a page search engines can find.

Reference Eventbrite link chips by place ↓ · Airbnb inspiration links ↓

Pros
  • Out of the way until someone has scrolled
  • Catches people who didn't find what they wanted
  • Good for search engines; reuses card tags
Cons
  • Only seen by people who scroll
  • Long rows of chips can look cluttered

These would use the same categories and tags as the chips on event cards, so the vocabulary is the same everywhere. This follows the search proposal's rule that new requests such as pujas, volunteering or teachings in French become queries or filters rather than header items.

Where every shortcut lands

Like the results banners below, this isn't a sixth option. Whichever option is chosen, its shortcuts, chips, suggestions and panel links all lead to the same place: the results page designed in the search proposal. It shows scope chips labelled from the header, with counts; teachers, centres and programmes above the results; dated results soonest first; and anytime content grouped separately. Getting this page right matters as much as the choice of navigation, because it's where every route ends up.

3

Scope chips carry the header's own labels and show counts, so a visitor can see at a glance where the matches actually are.

4

Entities sit above the results, not inside them. A teacher and a Tuesday evening class cannot be meaningfully ranked against each other.

5

Dated results sort soonest first, not by relevance. On a platform about what's coming up, the next thing is usually the answer.

Notes 3 to 5 are from the search proposal.

Adding context to results pages

This isn't an option in the same sense as the five above either. It's an opportunity that fits alongside any of them: giving the results page more character, and the visitor more context, depending on the filter they arrive with. Today a homepage icon leads to the general results page with one filter applied. On Eventbrite, a category or place leads to a page with its own banner and introduction, with results underneath (Refs. 6–8). For Lotus, a newcomer selecting Mindfulness could learn that it covers the more introductory side of Buddhist meditation, along with secular and scientific approaches, before seeing the list.

Reference Eventbrite category icons ↓ · Eventbrite landing page banner ↓ · Eventbrite categories within a landing page ↓

This doesn't need a separate results page for each category. The devs could show a different banner on the same results page depending on which category or location filter, or tag chip, is selected. Each banner then needs a short text and an image, which is a real content task as categories and traditions grow. IA v2 already gives each study programme its own landing page, for similar reasons: context for visitors and value in search.

Large retailers, universitiesMega menus, because the catalogue is large and visitors often don't know the right termsOption 2
Worth noting

None of the three event and travel platforms uses a mega menu in its header. They rely on search, scoped tabs and links on the page. The closest match in content, Wisdom Academy, does use one, organised by tradition. Mega menus are most common where the catalogue is large and unfamiliar. Lotus has some of both: a newcomer doesn't know the vocabulary, but the catalogue is still small.

Time shortcuts, in every option

Lotus has no quick way to filter by when today. Apart from "events this month" on the homepage, a visitor can only pick specific dates, and only once they're on the search page. The relative ranges people expect from sites like Eventbrite — Today, This weekend, This week, This month, Next month — don't exist yet.

Reference Eventbrite time chips ↓ · Eventbrite time tabs on the homepage ↓

Whichever direction is chosen, time shortcuts are one of the most useful things it can add.

Eventbrite pairs time with place on its homepage (Ref. 10): "Browsing events in" a location, then tabs for All, For you, Today and This weekend, directly under the category icons. Lotus could do the same under its own icon row. The shortcuts are worked out from the existing date filter, so they need no new data.

OptionWhere time shortcuts would appear
1 · Simple menuAs quick choices in the Date filter on the results page, and as tabs under the homepage icons
2 · Mega menuThe "When and where" column of the Events panel
3 · Search suggestionsAt the top of the dropdown when someone clicks into search
5 · Bottom-of-page linksA "By time" row of chips
Results bannersIn the filter bar under the banner, e.g. Mindfulness this weekend

What the walkthrough suggests

Experienced users and staff are served equally by every option. The difference is entirely about people who are still looking. The mega menu is strongest for showing breadth (Clara); the minimalist combination is strongest for visitors who arrive deep in the site (Sam); both clearly beat the simple menu alone for newcomers (Hana).

Searching with a term, and without one

The search proposal's field design assumes the visitor already has a word to type. Its example, "lamrim", counts as an exploration query in that proposal, but it still takes insider vocabulary to think of. That suits someone like Eric, who knows the teachings and the teachers.

Hana, Clara and Sam don't have that word yet. For them the useful moment is earlier, when the field is still empty: suggestions such as Near me, This weekend or Suitable for beginners give them a starting point without needing to know what to ask for. The two designs serve different people and can work together.

Two directions

Direction A · Minimalist

Simple menu, plus suggestions when searching, bottom-of-page links and results banners. The header stays calm. Guidance appears when someone searches, scrolls or picks a category, and every category gets context.

Direction B · Mega menu

The five-item header with panels on Events, Study and Retreats. Breadth and shortcuts are visible on every page. Results banners can still be added. Panels launch only with categories that have content.

The directions aren't mutually exclusive. Starting with A and adding panels later loses nothing, because every panel link would point at results pages and filters that A already needs.

How each direction relates to IA v2

Both directions build on IA v2 and the search proposal v1. Most of the options extend those documents rather than change them, but two points are worth raising before choosing.

What's a hub?

In IA v2, Study and Retreats are hubs: pages of their own, not just filters on the events list. A filter narrows a list that already exists, so a filter on the calendar can only show dated items. A hub brings everything for one intent together in sections, including undated content such as self-study and recorded retreats, and links to the calendar with a filter applied for anything dated. More detail: The IA v2 hub model, explained.

Two questions about the IA

Card or navigation. IA v2 resolves the confusion between events, study and retreats at the card, through mode badges and tags, rather than in the navigation. That is a good reason a simple header may be enough. A mega menu wouldn't replace the badges, but it would add a second layer of guidance, so it would extend IA v2 rather than just add a feature.

Hubs or filters. Option 4 would turn Study and Retreats into scopes on one search. IA v2 gives them their own hubs because they hold undated content too, so this option would change that model.

Same foundations either way

Whichever direction is chosen, the same groundwork sits underneath, and none of it needs deciding here. Every shortcut would use the vocabulary of the category proposal and land on the agreed global search. Once a direction is chosen, we can provide an exact map of the menu items and search filter options, what each represents in the data, and what it should show when clicked, as a baseline for the dev team to implement against.

Two points do affect the options. The homepage icons on staging are test content, and whether they show topics or content types is still open; the simple menu relies on them most. And the teaching archive has no link in the navigation yet, so whichever direction is chosen should give it a place under Study.

How to decide

Management makes the final call on direction and process, after the input listed first in the table.

WhoWhatWhen
Dev team BuildWhat each option would take to build, and which filters exist or need adding (tradition, organisation, retreat and event types). Also multi-session courses as one card, directory filters (#544) and usage tracking. Once a direction is chosen, an exact map of every menu item and search filter option, and its data, gives a baseline to implement againstFirst, and again once a direction is chosen
Everyone reviewing DiscussHow much guidance should the navigation itself give, and how much should come from search, filters and the pages people land on? Should Study and Retreats stay as pages of their own? Should the homepage icons show topics or content types?Before the decision
Mindful Design DesignReview tone and minimalism with RosieBefore the decision
Management Decide
  • Which options to take forward. Any combination of the five, not only A or B. For example, the minimalist combination, the mega menu, or A first with panels added later
  • Whether to mock up the shortlist in higher fidelity before committing, so the options can be compared as they would really look
  • When to open it up for feedback from centres and users: before launch, or after, as part of improving it over time
Once the input above is in
